findings.summary: In the safe-validation example, Vary: Origin is set only when the origin is allowed, which teaches a cache-poisoning gap.

findings.fix: Add a separate 'Telltale Signals' section or sub-heading before the signal bullets, so they read as detection cues and not as causes of lockout failing.

findings.summary: Detection signals are listed as flat bullets under the 'Why Lockout Misses It' heading without being separated, so detection signals read as part of the explanation of why lockout fails.
findings.evidence: No single IP or account trips a threshold / High login failure ratio / Many distinct usernames per IP or device fingerprint / Spike in 401s / Success rate only about 0.1-2%
findings.fix: Add a separate 'How to Detect It' section for the failure ratio, usernames per IP, 401 spike and success-rate bullets, and keep the lockout section to why thresholds are not tripped.

findings.summary: The 'Layered Defense' layers are bare words with no one-line explanation or visual, and the page names fewer layers than the cheat sheet's six.
findings.evidence: Throttle / Challenge / Second factor / Block known-bad passwords ... Stack all six layers (page 6)
findings.fix: Show the layers as a stacked diagram or a short table, with a one-line purpose for each. Name the same count and terms on pages 1 and 6.

findings.summary: The Redis counter code is shown before the idea behind it is stated, and the thresholds come only after the code.
findings.evidence: Store counters in Redis: INCR, then EXPIRE on first hit ... bash INCR fail:acct:alice ... 900 s = 15 min window
findings.fix: State the rule first ('5 failures per account and 20 per IP per 15 min, counted with INCR plus EXPIRE'), then show the code. Note that EXPIRE should be set only on the first hit, since the code as written resets the window each time.

findings.summary: One bullet packs several ideas: the header trust rule and the spoofing consequence are mixed, and 'Unknown and known usernames' joins two concerns, response and timing.
findings.evidence: Unknown and known usernames: same response and timing, no enumeration
findings.fix: Split into 'Same response for known and unknown usernames' and 'Same response time for both'.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "deliberately", "submitting").
findings.evidence: Lockout trade-off: it enables denial of service, because an attacker can deliberately lock out victims by submitting bad passwords
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The progressive delay is shown as a bare sequence with an ellipsis, and the page gives no hint of how to read it.
findings.evidence: 1s 2s 4s 8s ... 15 min cap
findings.fix: Label it as a delay-per-failed-attempt timeline, for example 'Failure 1 → 1s, 2 → 2s, 3 → 4s, 4 → 8s … capped at 15 min'.

findings.summary: The Interview Point block poses questions with answers that duplicate the trade-off table rather than adding to it.
findings.evidence: Delay vs lockout? Delay keeps access; lockout stops guessing but allows DoS.
findings.fix: Drop the Q&A that repeats the table, or keep one line that adds a new idea.

findings.summary: The CAPTCHA bullets mix the trigger rule, its cost to users and attacker bypass in one list, and a code block follows the flow diagram without a stated idea.
findings.evidence: Show it only after N failures or a high risk score / Solving farms and AI solvers win for a few cents per solve / bash curl -d "secret=$SECRET" ...
findings.fix: Group the bullets into 'When to show' and 'Limits', and add a one-line idea ('server verifies the token with the provider') before the curl.

findings.summary: The MFA table's Weakness column mixes a strength with weaknesses, and the gotcha bullets below repeat it.
findings.evidence: 1 | Passkeys / WebAuthn | phishing-resistant ... Approval spam wears users down on push / SIM-swap hijacks SMS codes
findings.fix: Name a real weakness for passkeys (device loss or recovery), and drop the bullets that duplicate the Push and SMS rows.

findings.summary: The range call output is shown without an explanation of what the 5-char prefix returns or how the full hash is compared, and the SHA-1 step is not stated before the curl.
findings.evidence: curl https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/21BD1 ... lines come back as SUFFIX:COUNT
findings.fix: State first that '21BD1' is the first 5 hex chars of the password's SHA-1 and the remaining 35 chars are compared locally, then show the call.

findings.summary: The NIST bullets are a separate policy topic placed inside the 'Policy on a hit' section, and 'Favour length; drop forced rotation and composition rules' holds two ideas.
findings.evidence: NIST 800-63B: block breached and common passwords / Favour length; drop forced rotation and composition rules
findings.fix: Move the NIST guidance to its own short section, and split the length rule from the rotation and composition rule.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet's Defaults table lacks a CAPTCHA/MFA row and the page says 'six layers' without numbering the layers.
findings.evidence: Stack all six layers ... Edge limit / Counters / Delay / CAPTCHA / MFA / Breach check
findings.fix: Number the layers 1-6 in the diagram, and reuse the page 1 wording for the layer names.

findings.summary: Answers for the self-check questions are given inline, with no separation from the questions, so a learner cannot test themselves.
findings.evidence: Does anything trip? No. Every account and every IP stays under its threshold.
findings.fix: Put each answer under an 'Answer:' label or in a Question | Answer table.

findings.summary: PKCE is used in the public/confidential table on page 1, but it is not introduced until page 2.
findings.evidence: "Authenticates with | PKCE, no secret | client_id + client_secret"
findings.fix: Add a short gloss on page 1, for example "PKCE: a one-time proof the client generates per login, replacing the secret (see page 2)".

findings.summary: Python code is shown after the step list but its one-line idea is only stated after the code.
findings.evidence:
python
import base64, hashlib, secrets ... 
S256 challenge: URL-safe base64, no = padding
findings.fix: Put the one-line idea (verifier -> SHA256 -> URL-safe base64 without padding) before the code block.

findings.summary: The four flow steps are a text list with long parameter dumps, and the browser/server actors are not shown, so the flow is hard to scan.
findings.evidence:
2. /authorize
response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, code_challenge, code_challenge_method=S256
findings.fix: Show the flow as a sequence diagram (client, auth server, user) and keep only the key parameters per step.

findings.summary: A bullet holds two ideas: PKCE rationale and when to use it.
findings.evidence: Use it for all clients; mandatory for public clients
findings.fix: Split into two bullets, or fold into the grant table as a separate column.

findings.summary: The ID token row and the refresh bullets pack several ideas into one cell or line.
findings.evidence: short-lived (minutes); issued once at login | client only; never an API credential
findings.fix: Move the extra facts into separate bullets or an extra table column.

findings.summary: The refresh request is shown as code, and the store/no-store advice is mixed into the Refresh section.
findings.evidence:
Store in httpOnly secure cookies or server-side
Never store tokens in localStorage: any XSS can read them
findings.fix: Move storage into its own heading, and state the refresh idea before the http block.

findings.summary: The outline's standard claims email and name are missing from the ID Token Claims table, so the claims-to-scope link is incomplete.
findings.evidence: The claims table lists only iss, sub, aud, exp/iat and nonce.
findings.fix: Add rows "email | user's email address (email scope)" and "name | display name (profile scope)".

findings.summary: Scope and claim tables are inconsistent: the scope table's Claims column mixes 'ID token' into the claims list.
findings.evidence: openid | sub, ID token
findings.fix: Make the openid row 'sub (required to get an ID token)'.

findings.summary: The nonce idea is repeated at the end of the discovery section, away from the claims table where it belongs.
findings.evidence: nonce ties the ID token to the request and stops replay
findings.fix: Remove it from section 3, since the claims table already covers nonce.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "verifying", "parameter").
findings.evidence: Mistake: skipping or not verifying the state parameter, which allows CSRF login attacks
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The SAML terms IdP, SP and ACS are used without being expanded or explained, so the table is hard to follow for a learner meeting SAML for the first time.
findings.evidence: "Roles | IdP and SP | Auth server and client" and "POSTed via browser to SP's ACS URL"
findings.fix: Add a line such as "IdP = Identity Provider (logs the user in); SP = Service Provider (the app); ACS = Assertion Consumer Service, the SP URL that receives the signed assertion."

findings.summary: A bullet holds multiple unrelated mistakes, and the IdP-initiated note lacks a clear link to the flow diagram.
findings.evidence: Tokens in localStorage, long-lived access tokens, over-broad scopes
findings.fix: One mistake per bullet, each with its consequence.

findings.summary: The quiz explanation says the verifier 'never left the client', but the verifier is sent to the server in the back-channel POST /token request.
findings.evidence: No: the verifier never left the client. Only its SHA256 code_challenge crossed the front channel
findings.fix: Say that the verifier never crosses the front channel. It is sent only in the back-channel /token call, so an attacker who has only the stolen code cannot supply it.

findings.summary: The first quiz explanation says the verifier 'never left the client', which contradicts the flow taught on page 2.
findings.evidence: "No: the verifier never left the client." Page 2 says: "POST /token ... code_verifier" and "The verifier travels only on the back channel."
findings.fix: Reword to: "No: the verifier is only ever sent on the back channel, so the attacker who saw the redirect never saw it. Only its SHA256 code_challenge crossed the front channel."
